name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q01 - Classification basis of plant tissues

questiontext.text: Plant tissues are broadly classified into two main groups, namely meristematic and permanent tissues, primarily on the basis of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A tissue is a group of cells having a common origin and usually performing a common function.

Step 2: Evaluation
Plants are made up of different kinds of tissues. Depending on whether the newly formed cells retain the capability of dividing or lose it after specialisation, plant tissues are divided into meristematic tissues (actively dividing) and permanent tissues (generally non-dividing).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the primary basis for classifying plant tissues into meristematic and permanent groups is whether the cells being formed are capable of dividing or not.

answer.text: Whether the cells being formed are capable of dividing or not
The chemical composition of their secondary cell walls
Their location in either the root system or the shoot system
The presence or absence of chloroplasts within the cells

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q02 - Location and role of apical meristems

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements accurately describes the location and function of apical meristems in flowering plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Growth in plants is largely restricted to specialised regions of active cell division called meristems.

Step 2: Evaluation
Apical meristems occur at the tips of roots and shoots (the distant-most region of the stem axis) and produce primary tissues, contributing to the formation of the primary plant body. Secondary tissues are produced by lateral meristems, not apical meristems.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, apical meristems occur at the tips of roots and shoots and produce primary tissues.

answer.text: They occur in the mature regions of woody axes and produce secondary tissues
They occur at the tips of roots and shoots and produce primary tissues
They occur exclusively between mature tissues in grasses to regenerate grazed parts
They are cylindrical meristems responsible for increasing the girth of stems

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q03 - Origin and potential of axillary buds

questiontext.text: During the formation of leaves and elongation of the stem, some cells 'left behind' from the shoot apical meristem constitute a structure present in the axils of leaves. This structure is the:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The shoot apical meristem occupies the distant-most region of the stem axis and gives rise to leaves and stem tissues.

Step 2: Evaluation
During leaf formation and stem elongation, some meristematic cells are left behind from the shoot apical meristem in the axils of leaves. These cells constitute the axillary bud, which is capable of forming a branch or a flower.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The structure formed by cells left behind from the shoot apical meristem in leaf axils is the axillary bud.

answer.text: Interfascicular cambium, capable of forming secondary xylem
Intercalary meristem, capable of regenerating leaf tips
Axillary bud, capable of forming a branch or a flower
Cork cambium, capable of forming protective periderm

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q04 - Intercalary meristem function in grasses

questiontext.text: In grasses, which meristematic tissue occurs between mature tissues and helps regenerate parts removed by grazing herbivores?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Primary meristems appear early in the life of a plant and contribute to the formation of the primary plant body.

Step 2: Evaluation
The meristem that occurs between mature tissues is known as the intercalary meristem. It is characteristically found in grasses and enables them to regenerate parts removed by grazing herbivores. Like apical meristems, intercalary meristems are primary meristems.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The meristem responsible for regenerating grazed parts in grasses is the intercalary meristem.

answer.text: Cork cambium
Root apical meristem
Fascicular vascular cambium
Intercalary meristem

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q05 - Examples of secondary lateral meristems

questiontext.text: Which of the following sets consists exclusively of secondary (lateral) meristems?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Secondary or lateral meristems are cylindrical meristems that occur in the mature regions of roots and shoots of many plants, particularly those producing a woody axis, and appear later than primary meristems.

Step 2: Evaluation
Fascicular vascular cambium, interfascicular cambium, and cork-cambium are all examples of lateral meristems responsible for producing secondary tissues. In contrast, shoot apical meristem, root apical meristem, and intercalary meristem are primary meristems.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the set consisting exclusively of secondary (lateral) meristems is fascicular vascular cambium, interfascicular cambium, and cork-cambium.

answer.text: Fascicular vascular cambium, interfascicular cambium, and cork-cambium
Apical meristem, intercalary meristem, and cork-cambium
Shoot apical meristem, root apical meristem, and interfascicular cambium
Intercalary meristem, axillary bud, and fascicular vascular cambium

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q06 - Differentiation of apical meristem into tissues

questiontext.text: Following cell divisions in primary and secondary meristems, the newly formed cells become structurally and functionally specialised and lose the ability to divide. Which of the following tissue groups are produced directly by specific regions of the apical meristem during the formation of the primary plant body?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Newly formed cells from meristems undergo specialisation to become permanent (mature) cells, forming the permanent tissues of the plant.

Step 2: Evaluation
During the formation of the primary plant body, specific regions of the apical meristem produce three primary tissue systems: dermal tissues, ground tissues, and vascular tissues. Secondary xylem, secondary phloem, and periderm are produced later by lateral meristems (vascular cambium and cork cambium).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, specific regions of the apical meristem produce dermal tissues, ground tissues, and vascular tissues.

answer.text: Secondary xylem, secondary phloem, and periderm
Dermal tissues, ground tissues, and vascular tissues
Phellem, phellogen, and phelloderm
Heartwood, sapwood, and lenticels

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q07 - Characteristics and functions of parenchyma

questiontext.text: Which simple permanent tissue forms the major component within plant organs, has thin cellulosic walls, generally isodiametric cells, and performs photosynthesis, storage, and secretion?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Simple permanent tissues consist of only one type of cell and include parenchyma, collenchyma, and sclerenchyma.

Step 2: Evaluation
Parenchyma forms the major component within plant organs. Its cells are generally isodiametric (spherical, oval, round, polygonal, or elongated) with thin walls made up of cellulose, either closely packed or with small intercellular spaces. Parenchyma performs functions such as photosynthesis, storage, and secretion.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The tissue described is parenchyma.

answer.text: Collenchyma
Sclerenchyma
Parenchyma
Xylem parenchyma

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q08 - Cell wall thickenings in collenchyma

questiontext.text: In collenchyma, the cells are much thickened at the corners due to the deposition of which combination of substances?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Collenchyma occurs in layers below the epidermis in most dicotyledonous plants, either as a homogeneous layer or in patches, providing mechanical support to growing parts.

Step 2: Evaluation
The cells of collenchyma are characteristically thickened at their corners due to a deposition of cellulose, hemicellulose, and pectin. Lignin is found in sclerenchyma, and suberin is found in endodermal casparian strips and cork cells.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The corner thickenings in collenchyma are composed of cellulose, hemicellulose, and pectin.

answer.text: Lignin, suberin, and cutin
Cellulose, lignin, and tannins
Suberin, pectin, and silica
Cellulose, hemicellulose, and pectin

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q09 - Chloroplasts and spaces in collenchyma

questiontext.text: Which of the following is true regarding collenchymatous cells in dicotyledonous plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Collenchyma is a living mechanical tissue found in young stems and petioles of leaves in most dicotyledonous plants.

Step 2: Evaluation
Collenchymatous cells may be oval, spherical, or polygonal and often contain chloroplasts; when they contain chloroplasts, they assimilate food. Intercellular spaces are absent in collenchyma.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, collenchymatous cells lack intercellular spaces and assimilate food when they contain chloroplasts.

answer.text: Intercellular spaces are absent, and they assimilate food when they contain chloroplasts
Large intercellular spaces are present, and the cells are dead at maturity
They are found exclusively in monocotyledonous roots and lack chloroplasts
They possess obliterated central lumens and highly lignified cell walls

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q10 - General characteristics of sclerenchyma

questiontext.text: Sclerenchyma consists of long, narrow cells that are usually dead and without protoplasts. Their cell walls are:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Sclerenchyma provides mechanical support to plant organs through thickened, rigid cell walls.

Step 2: Evaluation
Sclerenchyma cells have thick and lignified cell walls with a few or numerous pits. They are usually dead and devoid of protoplasts at maturity.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Their cell walls are thick and lignified with a few or numerous pits.

answer.text: Thin and made purely of cellulose without pits
Thick and lignified with a few or numerous pits
Thickened only at the corners with pectin and hemicellulose
Covered externally by a waxy cuticle layer

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q11 - Distinction between fibres and sclereids

questiontext.text: On the basis of variation in form, structure, origin, and development, sclerenchyma is classified into fibres and sclereids. How do sclereids differ from fibres?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Both fibres and sclereids are sclerenchymatous cells providing mechanical support, but they differ markedly in shape and lumen size.

Step 2: Evaluation
Fibres are thick-walled, elongated, and pointed cells generally occurring in groups. In contrast, sclereids are spherical, oval, or cylindrical, highly thickened dead cells with very narrow cavities (lumen).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Sclereids are spherical, oval, or cylindrical highly thickened dead cells with very narrow lumens.

answer.text: Sclereids are living cells with thin cellulosic walls, whereas fibres are dead
Sclereids are elongated with pointed ends, whereas fibres are spherical
Sclereids are spherical, oval, or cylindrical, highly thickened dead cells with very narrow lumens
Sclereids contain chloroplasts and perform photosynthesis, whereas fibres store starch

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q12 - Common locations of sclereids in plants

questiontext.text: Sclereids are commonly found in all of the following plant parts EXCEPT:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Sclereids are highly thickened, dead sclerenchymatous cells with very narrow lumens that provide hardness and mechanical protection.

Step 2: Evaluation
Sclereids are commonly found in the fruit walls of nuts, the pulp of fruits like guava, pear, and sapota, the seed coats of legumes, and the leaves of tea. They are not the cells constituting the root hairs of epiblema, which are unicellular elongations of living epidermal cells.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, unicellular root hairs of the epiblema do not contain sclereids.

answer.text: Fruit walls of nuts and seed coats of legumes
Pulp of fruits like guava, pear, and sapota
Leaves of tea
Unicellular root hairs of the epiblema

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q13 - Definition of complex permanent tissues

questiontext.text: Why are xylem and phloem classified as complex permanent tissues?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Permanent tissues are divided into simple and complex tissues based on whether they consist of a single cell type or multiple cell types.

Step 2: Evaluation
Complex tissues are made of more than one type of cell, and these different cell types work together as a single functional unit. Xylem (tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres, xylem parenchyma) and phloem (sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, phloem fibres) each consist of four different elements working together.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Xylem and phloem are called complex tissues because they are made of more than one type of cell working together as a unit.

answer.text: They are made of more than one type of cell working together as a unit
They are composed of actively dividing cells throughout the plant's life
All of their cells are identical in structure and lack cell walls
They are restricted solely to the leaves of angiosperms

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q14 - Xylem element absent in gymnosperms

questiontext.text: Which of the four xylem elements is characteristically present in angiosperms but absent in gymnosperms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Xylem is composed of four different kinds of elements: tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres, and xylem parenchyma.

Step 2: Evaluation
Gymnosperms lack vessels in their xylem. In contrast, the presence of vessels is a characteristic feature of angiosperms, where both tracheids and vessels serve as the main water-transporting elements.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The xylem element absent in gymnosperms and characteristic of angiosperms is vessels.

answer.text: Tracheids
Vessels
Xylem parenchyma
Xylem fibres

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q15 - Structure of tracheids and vessels

questiontext.text: How is a xylem vessel structurally organised in flowering plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Tracheids and vessels are the main water-transporting elements in flowering plants, both being dead and devoid of protoplasm at maturity.

Step 2: Evaluation
A vessel is a long cylindrical tube-like structure made up of many cells called vessel members, each with lignified walls and a large central cavity. These vessel members are interconnected through perforations in their common walls. Elongated cells with tapering ends describe tracheids, not vessels.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A vessel is a long cylindrical tube-like structure made up of many vessel members interconnected through perforations in their common walls.

answer.text: It is a single living cell with thin cellulosic walls and a large nucleus
It is an elongated unicellular structure with tapering ends and obliterated lumen
It is a long cylindrical tube-like structure of many vessel members interconnected through perforations
It is a septate sclerenchymatous fibre storing starch and tannins

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q16 - Living element of xylem and radial conduction

questiontext.text: Which element of xylem consists of living, thin-walled cells with cellulosic walls that store food materials (starch or fat) and tannins, and also assists in the radial conduction of water?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Among the four xylem elements—tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres, and xylem parenchyma—only one consists of living cells.

Step 2: Evaluation
Xylem parenchyma cells are living and thin-walled with cellulosic cell walls. They store food materials in the form of starch or fat, as well as substances like tannins. The radial conduction of water takes place via ray parenchymatous cells.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The living element of xylem described is xylem parenchyma.

answer.text: Tracheids
Vessel members
Xylem fibres
Xylem parenchyma

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q17 - Endarch and exarch primary xylem

questiontext.text: In roots, the protoxylem lies towards the periphery and the metaxylem lies towards the centre. This arrangement of primary xylem is termed:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Primary xylem consists of first-formed protoxylem and later-formed metaxylem, whose relative positions along the radius define two distinct patterns.

Step 2: Evaluation
When protoxylem lies towards the periphery and metaxylem lies towards the centre, as in roots, the arrangement is called exarch. Conversely, when protoxylem lies towards the centre (pith) and metaxylem lies towards the periphery, as in stems, it is called endarch.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The arrangement of primary xylem in roots is called exarch.

answer.text: Exarch
Endarch
Conjoint
Open

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q18 - Phloem elements in gymnosperms vs angiosperms

questiontext.text: Instead of sieve tubes and companion cells found in angiosperms, the phloem of gymnosperms possesses:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Phloem transports food materials, usually from leaves to other parts of the plant, and its cellular composition differs between angiosperms and gymnosperms.

Step 2: Evaluation
In angiosperms, phloem is composed of sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, and phloem fibres. Gymnosperms lack sieve tubes and companion cells; instead, they have albuminous cells and sieve cells.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Gymnosperms possess albuminous cells and sieve cells in their phloem.

answer.text: Vessel members and tracheids
Albuminous cells and sieve cells
Bulliform cells and subsidiary cells
Sclereids and complementary cells

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q19 - Features of mature sieve tube elements

questiontext.text: A mature sieve tube element in angiosperm phloem possesses:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Sieve tube elements are long, tube-like structures arranged longitudinally in angiosperm phloem, with end walls perforated in a sieve-like manner to form sieve plates.

Step 2: Evaluation
At maturity, a sieve element retains a peripheral cytoplasm and a large central vacuole, but lacks a nucleus. Because it lacks a nucleus, its functions are controlled by the nucleus of the closely associated companion cell.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A mature sieve tube element possesses a peripheral cytoplasm and a large vacuole, but lacks a nucleus.

answer.text: A prominent nucleus and dense cytoplasm without vacuoles
Lignified cell walls and no protoplasm at maturity
A peripheral cytoplasm and a large vacuole, but lacks a nucleus
Numerous chloroplasts and thick corner deposits of pectin

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q20 - Connection and function of companion cells

questiontext.text: How are companion cells connected to sieve tube elements, and what key physiological role do they perform in the sieve tubes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Companion cells are specialised parenchymatous cells closely associated with sieve tube elements in angiosperm phloem.

Step 2: Evaluation
Sieve tube elements and companion cells are connected by pit fields present between their common longitudinal walls. Functionally, companion cells control the activities of enucleated sieve tube elements and help in maintaining the pressure gradient in the sieve tubes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
They are connected by pit fields between their common longitudinal walls and help maintain the pressure gradient in the sieve tubes.

answer.text: Connected by sieve plates; store tannins and resins
Connected by casparian strips; conduct water radially
Connected by perforations in end walls; provide mechanical strength
Connected by pit fields between common longitudinal walls; maintain the pressure gradient

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q21 - Absence of phloem parenchyma in monocots

questiontext.text: Which statement accurately describes phloem parenchyma?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Phloem parenchyma consists of elongated, tapering cylindrical cells with dense cytoplasm and a nucleus, having cellulosic walls with pits for plasmodesmatal connections.

Step 2: Evaluation
Phloem parenchyma stores food material and other substances such as resins, latex, and mucilage. Notably, phloem parenchyma is absent in most of the monocotyledons.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Phloem parenchyma stores resins, latex, and mucilage, and is absent in most monocotyledons.

answer.text: It stores resins, latex, and mucilage, and is absent in most monocotyledons
It is made of dead sclerenchymatous cells and is absent in dicotyledons
It lacks a nucleus at maturity and forms sieve plates at its end walls
It is present exclusively in the secondary phloem of gymnosperms

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q22 - Phloem fibres and primary phloem types

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements about phloem fibres (bast fibres) and primary phloem is INCORRECT?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Phloem fibres are sclerenchymatous cells associated with phloem, and primary phloem is differentiated into protophloem and metaphloem.

Step 2: Evaluation
Phloem fibres are elongated, unbranched, pointed sclerenchymatous cells that lose protoplasm and become dead at maturity; those of jute, flax, and hemp are used commercially. They are generally absent in primary phloem and found in secondary phloem. Furthermore, protophloem has narrow sieve tubes, while metaphloem has bigger sieve tubes—so claiming protophloem has bigger sieve tubes than metaphloem is false.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The incorrect statement is that protophloem consists of bigger sieve tubes whereas metaphloem consists of narrow sieve tubes.

answer.text: Phloem fibres are generally absent in primary phloem but are found in secondary phloem
Protophloem consists of bigger sieve tubes whereas metaphloem consists of narrow sieve tubes
At maturity, phloem fibres lose their protoplasm and become dead
Phloem fibres of jute, flax, and hemp are used commercially

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q23 - Cuticle presence and function in plants

questiontext.text: The waxy thick layer called cuticle, which covers the outside of the epidermis to prevent water loss, is characteristically absent in:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The epidermis is the outermost single-layered protective covering of the primary plant body.

Step 2: Evaluation
On stems and leaves, the outside of the epidermis is often covered with a waxy thick layer called the cuticle, which prevents water loss. However, cuticle is absent in roots because roots must absorb water and minerals from the soil.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Cuticle is absent in roots.

answer.text: Dicotyledonous stems
Dorsiventral leaves
Roots
Isobilateral leaves

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q24 - Guard cell wall thickness and shape

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly describes the structure of guard cells in a stoma?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Stomata are structures in the epidermis of leaves that regulate transpiration and gaseous exchange.

Step 2: Evaluation
Each stoma is composed of two guard cells (bean-shaped in most plants, dumb-bell shaped in grasses) enclosing a stomatal pore. The outer walls of guard cells (away from the stomatal pore) are thin, while the inner walls (towards the stomatal pore) are highly thickened. Guard cells possess chloroplasts and regulate stomatal opening and closing.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Guard cells have thin outer walls, highly thickened inner walls, and possess chloroplasts.

answer.text: Outer walls are highly thickened, inner walls are thin, and chloroplasts are absent
Both outer and inner walls are uniformly thin, and chloroplasts are absent
Guard cells are always dumb-bell shaped in all dicots and monocots
Outer walls are thin, inner walls facing the pore are highly thickened, and chloroplasts are present

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q25 - Components of the stomatal apparatus

questiontext.text: The stomatal apparatus collectively consists of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Specialised epidermal cells in the vicinity of guard cells become modified in shape and size and are known as subsidiary cells.

Step 2: Evaluation
Together, the stomatal aperture (pore), the two guard cells, and the surrounding subsidiary cells constitute the stomatal apparatus.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The stomatal apparatus consists of the stomatal aperture, guard cells, and surrounding subsidiary cells.

answer.text: Stomatal aperture, guard cells, and surrounding subsidiary cells
Stomatal aperture, trichomes, and bulliform cells
Guard cells, bundle sheath cells, and mesophyll
Subsidiary cells, cuticle, and palisade parenchyma

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q26 - Root hairs versus shoot trichomes

questiontext.text: How do root hairs differ from trichomes of the shoot system?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Epidermal cells bear appendages such as root hairs on roots and trichomes on stems.

Step 2: Evaluation
Root hairs are unicellular elongations of epidermal cells that help absorb water and minerals from the soil. In contrast, trichomes in the shoot system are usually multicellular (branched or unbranched, soft or stiff, sometimes secretory) and help prevent water loss due to transpiration.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Root hairs are unicellular and absorb water and minerals, whereas trichomes are usually multicellular and help prevent water loss.

answer.text: Root hairs are multicellular and secretory, whereas trichomes are unicellular
Root hairs are unicellular and absorb water and minerals, whereas trichomes are usually multicellular and prevent water loss
Root hairs prevent transpiration, whereas trichomes absorb minerals from the atmosphere
Both root hairs and trichomes are exclusively unicellular and dead at maturity

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q27 - Ground tissue system and vascular bundles

questiontext.text: Which tissues are excluded from the ground tissue system of a flowering plant?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
On the basis of structure and location, plants have three tissue systems: epidermal, ground (fundamental), and vascular (conducting).

Step 2: Evaluation
All tissues except the epidermis and vascular bundles constitute the ground tissue. In primary stems and roots, ground tissue includes cortex, pericycle, pith, and medullary rays; in leaves, it consists of thin-walled chloroplast-containing cells called mesophyll.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The epidermis and vascular bundles are excluded from the ground tissue system.

answer.text: Cortex and pericycle
Pith and medullary rays
Epidermis and vascular bundles
Mesophyll and cortex

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q28 - Casparian strips in dicot root endodermis

questiontext.text: In a dicotyledonous root, the casparian strips are formed by the deposition of water-impermeable suberin on the:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The innermost layer of the cortex in a dicotyledonous root is the endodermis, comprising a single layer of barrel-shaped cells without intercellular spaces.

Step 2: Evaluation
Both the tangential as well as radial walls of the endodermal cells have a deposition of the water-impermeable, waxy material suberin in the form of casparian strips.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Casparian strips are deposited on the tangential as well as radial walls of endodermal cells.

answer.text: Outer walls of the epiblema cells only
Corners of hypodermal collenchyma cells
Perforation plates of xylem vessel members
Tangential as well as radial walls of endodermal cells

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q29 - Pericycle role and stele in dicot root

questiontext.text: In a dicotyledonous root, initiation of lateral roots and vascular cambium during secondary growth takes place in the:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
All tissues on the inner side of the endodermis—namely pericycle, vascular bundles, and pith—constitute the stele.

Step 2: Evaluation
Next to the endodermis lies a few layers of thick-walled parenchymatous cells referred to as the pericycle. In dicot roots, the initiation of lateral roots and the vascular cambium during secondary growth takes place in these pericycle cells (along with conjunctive tissue below phloem bundles).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Initiation of lateral roots and vascular cambium during secondary growth occurs in the pericycle.

answer.text: Pericycle
Epiblema
Endodermis
Cortex

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q30 - Distinguishing monocot root from dicot root

questiontext.text: How does the internal anatomy of a monocotyledonous root differ from that of a dicotyledonous root?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Both monocot and dicot roots share epidermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle, radial exarch vascular bundles, and pith, but differ in bundle number, pith size, and secondary growth.

Step 2: Evaluation
Dicot roots usually have two to four xylem and phloem patches, a small or inconspicuous pith, and undergo secondary growth. Monocot roots usually have more than six (polyarch) xylem bundles, a large and well-developed pith, and do not undergo any secondary growth.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A monocot root has polyarch xylem bundles (more than six), a large well-developed pith, and no secondary growth.

answer.text: Monocot roots have two to four xylem bundles, an inconspicuous pith, and undergo secondary growth
Monocot roots have more than six (polyarch) xylem bundles, a large well-developed pith, and no secondary growth
Monocot roots lack endodermis and pericycle, and have endarch xylem
Monocot roots have conjoint open vascular bundles arranged in a ring

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q31 - Three sub-zones of dicot stem cortex

questiontext.text: In a typical young dicotyledonous stem, the cortex located between the epidermis and pericycle consists of three sub-zones. From outside to inside, these three sub-zones are:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a dicotyledonous stem, multiple layers of cells between the epidermis and pericycle constitute the cortex.

Step 2: Evaluation
1. The outer hypodermis consists of a few layers of collenchymatous cells just below the epidermis, providing mechanical strength.
2. Below the hypodermis lie cortical layers of rounded, thin-walled parenchymatous cells with conspicuous intercellular spaces.
3. The innermost layer of the cortex is the endodermis, whose cells are rich in starch grains and hence also called the starch sheath.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
From outside to inside, the three sub-zones are collenchymatous hypodermis, parenchymatous cortical layers, and the starch sheath (endodermis).

answer.text: Sclerenchymatous hypodermis, medullary rays, and casparian endodermis
Parenchymatous hypodermis, collenchymatous cortex, and pericycle
Collenchymatous hypodermis, parenchymatous cortical layers, and starch sheath (endodermis)
Starch sheath, sclerenchymatous pericycle, and parenchymatous pith

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q32 - Pericycle and vascular bundles in dicot stem

questiontext.text: In a dicotyledonous stem, the pericycle is present on the inner side of the endodermis and above the phloem in the form of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A dicotyledonous stem has vascular bundles arranged in a characteristic ring, each being conjoint, open, and with endarch protoxylem.

Step 2: Evaluation
On the inner side of the endodermis (starch sheath) and directly above the phloem of each vascular bundle, the pericycle is present in the form of semi-lunar patches of sclerenchyma.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The pericycle in a dicot stem occurs as semi-lunar patches of sclerenchyma.

answer.text: A continuous single layer of thin-walled parenchyma
Barrel-shaped cells with suberised casparian strips
Radially placed collenchymatous medullary rays
Semi-lunar patches of sclerenchyma

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q33 - Identifying features of monocot stem

questiontext.text: A transverse section of a plant stem shows a sclerenchymatous hypodermis, scattered conjoint closed vascular bundles surrounded by sclerenchymatous bundle sheaths, absence of phloem parenchyma, and water-containing cavities within the vascular bundles. This specimen is a:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Monocotyledonous and dicotyledonous stems are anatomically distinct in their hypodermis, vascular bundle arrangement, bundle sheath, phloem parenchyma, and ground tissue.

Step 2: Evaluation
A monocotyledonous stem characteristically has a sclerenchymatous hypodermis, numerous scattered conjoint and closed vascular bundles (each surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath, with peripheral bundles smaller than central ones), a large conspicuous parenchymatous ground tissue, absence of phloem parenchyma, and water-containing cavities within the vascular bundles.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The described stem is a monocotyledonous stem.

answer.text: Monocotyledonous stem
Dicotyledonous stem
Monocotyledonous root
Dicotyledonous root

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q34 - Stomatal distribution in dorsiventral leaf

questiontext.text: In a dorsiventral (dicotyledonous) leaf, stomata are:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A dorsiventral leaf has an upper (adaxial) epidermis and a lower (abaxial) epidermis, both covered by a conspicuous cuticle.

Step 2: Evaluation
In a dorsiventral leaf, the abaxial (lower) epidermis generally bears more stomata than the adaxial (upper) epidermis. In fact, the adaxial epidermis may even lack stomata.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Stomata are generally more numerous on the abaxial epidermis than on the adaxial epidermis.

answer.text: Present in equal numbers on both adaxial and abaxial surfaces
Generally more numerous on the abaxial epidermis than on the adaxial epidermis
Restricted exclusively to the adaxial epidermis
Completely absent from both epidermal surfaces

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q35 - Mesophyll differentiation in dorsiventral leaf

questiontext.text: In a dorsiventral leaf, the mesophyll is differentiated into palisade parenchyma and spongy parenchyma. Which statement accurately describes their arrangement?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The mesophyll between the upper and lower epidermis of a dorsiventral leaf is made of chloroplast-containing parenchyma cells that carry out photosynthesis.

Step 2: Evaluation
The palisade parenchyma is adaxially placed (towards the upper epidermis) and consists of elongated cells arranged vertically and parallel to each other. Below the palisade cells lies the spongy parenchyma, consisting of oval or round, loosely arranged cells with numerous large spaces and air cavities extending to the lower (abaxial) epidermis.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Palisade parenchyma is adaxially placed with vertically parallel elongated cells, while spongy parenchyma is loosely arranged below it with large air cavities.

answer.text: Spongy parenchyma is adaxially placed and consists of vertically elongated cells
Palisade parenchyma is abaxially placed and contains large intercellular air cavities
Palisade parenchyma is adaxially placed with vertically parallel elongated cells, and spongy parenchyma lies below it
Both palisade and spongy parenchyma are made of dead sclerenchymatous cells

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q36 - Characteristic features of isobilateral leaf

questiontext.text: Which combination of anatomical features is characteristic of an isobilateral (monocotyledonous) leaf?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An isobilateral (monocotyledonous) leaf shares basic tissue systems with a dorsiventral leaf but exhibits key anatomical differences.

Step 2: Evaluation
In an isobilateral leaf, stomata are present on both surfaces of the epidermis, and the mesophyll is not differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma. Additionally, parallel venation is reflected in the near-similar sizes of vascular bundles (except in main veins) seen in vertical sections.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Stomata on both epidermal surfaces, undifferentiated mesophyll, and near-similar vascular bundle sizes due to parallel venation characterise an isobilateral leaf.

answer.text: Stomata only on abaxial surface, differentiated mesophyll, and varying bundle sizes
Stomata only on adaxial surface, undifferentiated mesophyll, and reticulate venation
Stomata on both surfaces, differentiated palisade and spongy layers, and open vascular bundles
Stomata on both surfaces, undifferentiated mesophyll, and near-similar vascular bundle sizes

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q37 - Bulliform cells response to water stress

questiontext.text: In grasses, certain adaxial epidermal cells along the veins modify into large, empty, colourless bulliform cells. When these cells become flaccid due to water stress, they:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Bulliform cells in grass leaves respond to changes in water availability to regulate leaf surface exposure.

Step 2: Evaluation
When bulliform cells have absorbed water and are turgid, the leaf surface is exposed. When they become flaccid due to water stress, they cause the leaves to curl inwards to minimise water loss through transpiration.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Flaccid bulliform cells make the leaves curl inwards to minimise water loss.

answer.text: Make the leaves curl inwards to minimise water loss
Keep the leaf surface fully exposed to maximise photosynthesis
Rupture the epidermis to form lenticels for gaseous exchange
Secrete suberin to block the stomatal pore

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q38 - Lateral meristems in secondary growth

questiontext.text: Secondary growth in most dicotyledonous plants increases the girth of roots and stems through the activity of which two lateral meristems?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Primary growth increases the length of roots and stems via apical meristems, whereas secondary growth increases girth.

Step 2: Evaluation
The two lateral meristems involved in secondary growth are the vascular cambium and the cork cambium. Secondary growth occurs in dicots and gymnosperms, but does not occur in monocotyledons.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Secondary growth is brought about by the vascular cambium and cork cambium.

answer.text: Apical meristem and intercalary meristem
Vascular cambium and cork cambium
Root apical meristem and pericycle
Intercalary meristem and phelloderm

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q39 - Origin of interfascicular cambium in stem

questiontext.text: During secondary growth in a dicotyledonous stem, a continuous cambial ring is formed when cells adjoining the intrafascicular cambium become meristematic to form the interfascicular cambium. Which cells give rise to the interfascicular cambium?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In young dicot stems, vascular cambium is initially present in patches between primary xylem and primary phloem as intrafascicular cambium.

Step 2: Evaluation
To complete a continuous cambial ring, the cells of the medullary rays adjoining the intrafascicular cambium become meristematic (dedifferentiate) and form the interfascicular cambium.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Interfascicular cambium originates from the cells of the medullary rays.

answer.text: Cells of the endodermal starch sheath
Sclerenchymatous cells of the pericycle
Cells of the medullary rays
Collenchymatous cells of the hypodermis

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q40 - Secondary medullary rays and xylem accumulation

questiontext.text: During the activity of the vascular cambial ring in a dicot stem, what is the fate of primary and secondary phloems, and what are the narrow bands of parenchyma passing radially through secondary xylem and phloem called?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The cambial ring cuts off secondary xylem towards the pith and secondary phloem towards the periphery, and is generally more active on the inner side than on the outer side.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because far more secondary xylem is produced, it forms a compact mass that gradually crushes the primary and secondary phloems, while primary xylem remains more or less intact in or around the centre. At some places, the cambium forms a narrow band of parenchyma passing radially through the secondary xylem and secondary phloem; these are called secondary medullary rays.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Primary and secondary phloems get gradually crushed, and the radial parenchymatous bands are called secondary medullary rays.

answer.text: Phloems remain intact; radial bands are called casparian strips
Phloems differentiate into heartwood; radial bands are called phelloderm
Phloems convert into sclereids; radial bands are called conjunctive tissue
Phloems get gradually crushed; radial bands are called secondary medullary rays

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q41 - Spring wood versus autumn wood characteristics

questiontext.text: In temperate regions, how does spring wood (early wood) differ from autumn wood (late wood)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cambial activity is influenced by seasonal climatic changes in temperate regions, producing two distinct types of wood that form an annual ring.

Step 2: Evaluation
In spring, cambium is very active and produces numerous xylary elements having vessels with wider cavities; this spring wood is lighter in colour and has a lower density. In winter, cambium is less active and forms fewer xylary elements with narrow vessels; this autumn wood is darker and has a higher density.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Spring wood has wider vessels, lighter colour, and lower density compared to autumn wood.

answer.text: Spring wood has wider vessels, lighter colour, and lower density than autumn wood
Spring wood has narrow vessels, darker colour, and higher density than autumn wood
Spring wood is formed when cambium is less active in winter
Spring wood consists exclusively of secondary phloem, whereas autumn wood is secondary xylem

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q42 - Composition and resistance of heartwood

questiontext.text: Why is the central heartwood of old trees hard, durable, and resistant to the attacks of micro-organisms and insects?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In old trees, the central or innermost layers of secondary xylem undergo chemical and structural changes to form dark brown heartwood.

Step 2: Evaluation
Organic compounds such as tannins, resins, oils, gums, aromatic substances, and essential oils are deposited in the central layers of secondary xylem. These depositions make heartwood hard, durable, and resistant to micro-organisms and insects. Heartwood comprises dead elements with highly lignified walls and does not conduct water.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Heartwood is durable and resistant due to the deposition of tannins, resins, oils, gums, aromatic substances, and essential oils.

answer.text: Due to active water conduction through living ray parenchyma
Due to deposition of tannins, resins, oils, gums, aromatic substances, and essential oils
Due to accumulation of starch grains in the endodermal sheath
Due to high turgor pressure maintained by companion cells

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q43 - Function of sapwood in old trees

questiontext.text: Which region of the secondary xylem in old trees is lighter in colour and actively involved in the conduction of water and minerals from root to leaf?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Secondary xylem in old woody stems is differentiated into central heartwood and peripheral sapwood.

Step 2: Evaluation
While heartwood is dark brown and non-conducting, the peripheral region of the secondary xylem is lighter in colour and is known as sapwood. Sapwood is directly involved in conducting water and minerals from the root to the leaf.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The peripheral, lighter-coloured, water-conducting region of secondary xylem is sapwood.

answer.text: Heartwood
Phellem
Sapwood
Phelloderm

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q44 - Derivatives of cork cambium phellogen

questiontext.text: Cork cambium (phellogen), which usually develops in the cortex region, cuts off cells on both sides. Its outer and inner derivatives differentiate respectively into:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cork cambium (phellogen) is a couple of layers thick and consists of narrow, thin-walled, nearly rectangular meristematic cells.

Step 2: Evaluation
Phellogen divides to cut off cells on both sides: the outer cells differentiate into cork (phellem), while the inner cells differentiate into secondary cortex (phelloderm).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The outer derivatives form cork (phellem) and the inner derivatives form secondary cortex (phelloderm).

answer.text: Outer secondary cortex (phelloderm) and inner cork (phellem)
Outer secondary phloem and inner secondary xylem
Outer epidermis and inner endodermis
Outer cork (phellem) and inner secondary cortex (phelloderm)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q45 - Composition of periderm and cork impermeability

questiontext.text: Which three layers are collectively known as periderm, and why is the cork layer impervious to water?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Periderm replaces the broken outer cortical and epidermal layers during secondary growth in woody stems.

Step 2: Evaluation
Phellogen (cork cambium), phellem (cork), and phelloderm (secondary cortex) are collectively known as periderm. The cork (phellem) is impervious to water due to the deposition of suberin in its cell walls.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Periderm consists of phellogen, phellem, and phelloderm, and cork is impervious to water due to suberin deposition.

answer.text: Phellogen, phellem, and phelloderm; cork is impervious due to suberin deposition
Epidermis, hypodermis, and endodermis; cork is impervious due to lignin deposition
Secondary xylem, vascular cambium, and secondary phloem; cork is impervious due to pectin deposition
Phellogen, pericycle, and pith; cork is impervious due to tannin deposition

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q46 - Non-technical term bark and its types

questiontext.text: In woody stems, the non-technical term 'bark' refers to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Bark is a broad, non-technical anatomical term used for the outer protective and conducting tissues of a woody stem.

Step 2: Evaluation
Bark refers to all tissues exterior to the vascular cambium, therefore including the secondary phloem and the periderm (phellogen, phellem, and phelloderm). Bark formed early in the season is called early or soft bark, while that formed towards the end of the season is called late or hard bark.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Bark refers to all tissues exterior to the vascular cambium, including periderm and secondary phloem.

answer.text: Only the dead phellem cells sloughed off outside the phellogen
All tissues exterior to the vascular cambium, including periderm and secondary phloem
All tissues interior to the vascular cambium, including heartwood and sapwood
Only the primary cortex and epidermis of a young herbaceous stem

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q47 - Formation and function of lenticels

questiontext.text: At certain regions in woody trees, phellogen cuts off closely arranged parenchymatous cells on the outer side instead of cork cells. These cells rupture the epidermis to form lens-shaped openings called lenticels, which function in:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Because suberised cork (phellem) is impervious to water and gases, woody stems require specialised openings for aeration of internal living tissues.

Step 2: Evaluation
At certain regions, phellogen cuts off closely arranged parenchymatous complementary cells on the outer side instead of cork cells. These cells soon rupture the epidermis, forming lens-shaped openings called lenticels, which permit the exchange of gases between the outer atmosphere and the internal tissue of the stem.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Lenticels function in the exchange of gases between the outer atmosphere and internal stem tissues.

answer.text: Radial translocation of photosynthates from leaves to roots
Initiation of lateral roots during secondary growth
Exchange of gases between the outer atmosphere and internal stem tissues
Preventing water loss by secreting a thick waxy cuticle

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANATOMYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q48 - Origin of vascular cambium in dicot roots

questiontext.text: In a dicotyledonous root, the vascular cambium is completely secondary in origin. From which tissues does it originate to form a continuous wavy ring?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Unlike dicot stems where intrafascicular cambium is already present in primary vascular bundles, dicot roots have radial vascular bundles lacking primary cambium.

Step 2: Evaluation
In the dicot root, the vascular cambium originates completely secondarily from the tissue located just below the phloem bundles (conjunctive tissue) and a portion of pericycle tissue located above the protoxylem. Together, these form a complete and continuous wavy ring, which later becomes circular.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The vascular cambium in dicot roots originates from the tissue just below the phloem bundles and a portion of pericycle tissue above the protoxylem.

answer.text: Intrafascicular cambium and medullary ray cells
Epiblema and outer cortical parenchyma cells
Endodermis and central pith cells
Tissue just below the phloem bundles and a portion of pericycle above the protoxylem
